scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Yove male mome, also known as Povela e Yova, originates from the traditional dance Jove from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria.
In 1966, US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell introduced its choreography outside of Bulgaria at an event in Stockton, California.
Following this introduction, the dance became widely popular among international folk dancers across the globe.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally danced to communal folk songs in the Shopluk region, the dance is tied to the lyrical narrative of Yova watering horses—giving clear water to her beloved's horse and murky water to her brother's horse.
Today, it is widely performed at folk dance clubs, workshops, and recreational Balkan dance gatherings worldwide.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a fast, complicated line dance arranged in a curved line or open circle.
Dancers link together by holding their neighbours by the belt, or by the hands if belts are not worn.
Structurally, one common version consists of seven patterns containing four bars each.
Watch for Belt-hold line travel, Seven-pattern sequence.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Musical renditions of Yove male mome are played in an 18/16 compound meter (7+11/16), incorporating alternating sub-bars of common chetvorno (7/16) and kopanitsa (11/16) rhythms.
The melody and accompaniment often feature the traditional Bulgarian gaida (bagpipe).
Listen for the gaida.

A rapid, driving compound meter combining a 7/16 chetvorno rhythm and an 11/16 kopanitsa rhythm. The acoustic landscape is anchored by the droning reeds and ornamentation of the Bulgarian gaida over an asymmetric pulsing pulse of slow and quick subdivisions.

scenes.title: The people
narration: US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell played a pivotal role in disseminating the dance by introducing its choreography outside Bulgaria in Stockton, California, in 1966.
Folklorist Manol Todorov documented the song's lyrics in his 1976 work Balgarska narodna muzika, and Bulgarian singer Hristina Boteva is known for performing the song.
The dance originates from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria under the traditional name Jove.
Yove male mome derives directly from the regional Shopluk dance Jove.

scenes.title: Family tree

Yove male mome is influence of Chetvorno: Supplies the 7/16 rhythmic component of the 18/16 compound meter.
Yove male mome is influence of Kopanitsa: Supplies the 11/16 rhythmic component of the 18/16 compound meter.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Execute the 7/16 sub-bar with a slow step on count 1 (three pulses) followed by two quick steps on counts 2 and 3 (two pulses each).
